content:
United Independent School District and Laredo College have celebrated a first: the inaugural cohort of their Commercial Driver's License (CDL) Program, with all 11 students earning their Professional Truck Driver Certification — a 100% passing rate.

The 11 students came from United High School, United South High School, Lyndon B. Johnson High School and J.B. Alexander High School, and were honored in a ceremony surrounded by their families, instructors and school leaders. Launched this year through a partnership between United ISD and Laredo College, the program lets students earn an industry-recognized certification and gain workforce experience before graduating high school.

“Today, we had the pleasure of celebrating 11 students from the first cohort of our new CDL Program,” said Claudia Gonzalez, United ISD Director of Career and Technical Education (CTE). “With the support of Laredo College, Dr. Cruz, our Board of Trustees, and everyone involved, we were able to provide our students with this opportunity. Logistics is a major part of Laredo's economy, and the demand for commercial drivers remains very high.” Gonzalez also recognized Board Secretary Michelle Molina for her support in bringing the program to fruition.

The program is the newest addition to United ISD's more than 30 Career and Technical Education programs of study, spanning all 14 state-approved career clusters — from architecture, HVAC and diesel technology to health science, graphic design and video game design.

For United South High School graduate Julio Cesar Martinez Jr., the certification was a way to honor his father, who passed away earlier this year. The two had talked all his life about one day obtaining a CDL. “I wanted to do it for him. Now that I did it, I feel like I completed something that I've been waiting for my whole life,” he shared. Training, he noted, is expensive — “but thankfully, with UISD's help, we were able to do it completely free.” He hopes to pursue a career as a tanker driver in the oil field.

For Lyndon B. Johnson High School student Derek Palencia, trucking has been part of life since childhood — at age 10 he began traveling alongside his father in his semi-truck. He praised the program's driving simulator, which exposed students to severe weather and roadway hazards, and the challenge of maneuvering, parking and reversing a 53-foot trailer. “Once I turn 21, I want to become a truck driver, save my money, buy my own truck, and start my own company with my dad,” he said.

“Each of these students has worked hard to get to this moment, and their journeys look different,” Superintendent Dr. Gerardo Cruz shared. “Some are honoring family members, others are following traditions that began long before they entered this program, but all of them have shown resilience and determination. We are excited to see where their paths lead.”
